scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire document is an EHR-based retrospective cohort study (RECOVER Initiative, N3C/PCORnet/PEDSnet) measuring long COVID incidence proportions in adults and children between 2020 and 2024; Lyme disease is not mentioned anywhere in the text, tables, or figures.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This peer-reviewed study used electronic health record data from three large U.S. research networks (N3C, PCORnet, PEDSnet) covering over 6.3 million COVID-19-positive adults and children to estimate how many developed long COVID within 180 days of infection, using each network's own computer-based case definition. It found that 10.2%-25.9% of adults and 4.0% of children were identified as having probable long COVID, with lower 'excess incidence' estimates (5%-6% in adults, 1.4% in children) after subtracting background rates seen in COVID-negative control groups. The study reports who bears higher risk (older adults, women, people with more severe acute COVID-19 or more pre-existing conditions) and finds no decline in incidence through January 2024. The paper does not report any dollar costs, direct or indirect financial burden, insurance/access barriers, or caregiving-time measures - it is purely an epidemiological incidence study.

contextual_issues: The Introduction states (citing a separate study, Tartof et al. 2022, not a finding of this document itself) that long COVID 'can profoundly impact quality of life and lead to functional limitations, psychological distress, and higher numbers of healthcare visits' - this document does not itself measure or quantify these impacts.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost, direct non-medical cost (travel, paid help), indirect cost (lost income, productivity loss, caregiving time), or insurance/access-barrier cost data of any kind appear anywhere in this document - it reports incidence proportions only, no dollar figures or price year.

No data on repeated care-seeking patterns, length of diagnostic delay, or number/sequence of healthcare encounters specific to long COVID patients is quantified beyond the EHR visit-based case-ascertainment criteria themselves.
No Lyme disease content of any kind is present; this document cannot support any Lyme disease burden modeling, comparison, or crosscheck.

No caregiver time, household/family financial impact, or long-term (multi-year) financial consequence data are reported; the study's longest follow-up window used for incidence ascertainment is 270 days (harmonized analysis) or 180 days (main analysis), not a lifetime or multi-year cost horizon.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool the N3C (3,800,805 adults), PCORnet (1,870,810 adults), and PEDSnet (727,994 children) incidence estimates as a single range implying comparable measurement: each network applied a structurally different computable phenotype (N3C: machine-learning model trained on patients diagnosed with long COVID twice or with ≥2 long COVID clinic visits; PCORnet and PEDSnet: rules-based ICD-10 diagnosis-cluster algorithms) to different-sized, differently defined cohorts (adults vs. children).

Do not pool crude incidence proportion (10.2%-25.9% adults; 4.0% children) with excess incidence (5.3%-6.3% adults; 1.4% children) as if they were the same quantity at different confidence levels - excess incidence subtracts a COVID-negative control group's background rate and is explicitly presented by the authors as a 'lower bound' estimate, a conceptually different quantity from crude incidence.

The harmonized NASEM-aligned adult estimates (N3C 12.6%; PCORnet 9.6%) used a 270-day incidence window and were applied only to the two adult networks (not PEDSnet) - do not place these alongside the main 180-day-window estimates in a single low-to-high range without noting the different time window, different (harmonized) case definition, and exclusion of the pediatric network.

The 'historical' (Jan-May 2019) and 'contemporary' (Jan-May 2021) COVID-negative control groups are different populations drawn from different time periods used only to approximate a 'baseline' burden of long-COVID-like symptoms; the authors themselves note contemporary controls may have undocumented infections (understating the baseline) while historical controls may have different healthcare-utilization patterns (overstating the baseline) - neither should be treated as a nationally representative comparison population.

sex_gender_findings.finding: Across all three networks, female patients had a significantly higher adjusted risk of developing long COVID than male patients (N3C adjusted hazard ratio 1.41 [95% CI 1.41-1.42]; PCORnet adjusted hazard ratio 1.14 [1.12-1.14]; PEDSnet adjusted hazard ratio 1.17 [1.14-1.22]).

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: This study's long COVID case definitions are themselves built on ICD-10 diagnosis codes and EHR documentation: N3C's definition uses U09.9/B94.8 codes and a machine-learning model trained on patients diagnosed with U09.9 at least twice or who visited a long COVID clinic at least twice; PCORnet and PEDSnet use rules-based ICD-10 diagnosis-cluster algorithms. The document's own Limitations section states that EHR data 'may lead to underreporting or missed diagnoses of COVID-19 and long COVID, especially as patients must seek care as a prerequisite for having documentation available,' and that findings 'may also be influenced by...variation in healthcare access by gender, race/ethnicity, rurality, and other structural or social determinants of health.'

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document describes a classification/measurement-standard gap: there is no gold-standard, unified case definition for long COVID, each EHR research network built and applied its own computable phenotype, and the U09.9 ICD-10 code itself was introduced only partway through the study period with its adoption and use varying by healthcare institution - meaning no single, consistent diagnostic coding pathway existed across the health system during the study period.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: The document states: 'Given the lack of a gold standard, various case definitions for long COVID have been operationalized by researchers' (Introduction) and 'The code U09.9 was not appropriate for this purpose, as it was introduced during the study period and its adoption and use varies by healthcare institution' (Harmonized Long COVID Outcome Analysis, Methods).

federal_evidence_used.how_used: Used only to independently confirm that U09.9 (post COVID-19 condition) is the ICD-10-CM code referenced in this document's N3C/PCORnet/PEDSnet case definitions, and that B94.8 (sequelae of other specified infectious and parasitic diseases) is a nonspecific code also used in case ascertainment - supporting the claims_undercounting_caveat. This federal file contains no long COVID patient counts or costs and was not used to ground any crosscheck value.

scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire document is an EHR-based retrospective cohort study (RECOVER Initiative, N3C/PCORnet/PEDSnet) measuring long COVID incidence proportions in adults and children between 2020 and 2024; Lyme disease is not mentioned anywhere in the text, tables, or figures.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This peer-reviewed study used electronic health record data from three large U.S. research networks (N3C, PCORnet, PEDSnet) covering over 6.3 million COVID-19-positive adults and children to estimate how many developed long COVID within 180 days of infection, using each network's own computer-based case definition. It found that 10.2%-25.9% of adults and 4.0% of children were identified as having probable long COVID, with lower 'excess incidence' estimates (5%-6% in adults, 1.4% in children) after subtracting background rates seen in COVID-negative control groups. The study reports who bears higher risk (older adults, women, people with more severe acute COVID-19 or more pre-existing conditions) and finds no decline in incidence through January 2024. The paper does not report any dollar costs, direct or indirect financial burden, insurance/access barriers, or caregiving-time measures - it is purely an epidemiological incidence study.

contextual_issues: The Introduction states (citing a separate study, Tartof et al. 2022, not a finding of this document itself) that long COVID 'can profoundly impact quality of life and lead to functional limitations, psychological distress, and higher numbers of healthcare visits' - this document does not itself measure or quantify these impacts.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost, direct non-medical cost (travel, paid help), indirect cost (lost income, productivity loss, caregiving time), or insurance/access-barrier cost data of any kind appear anywhere in this document - it reports incidence proportions only, no dollar figures or price year.

No data on repeated care-seeking patterns, length of diagnostic delay, or number/sequence of healthcare encounters specific to long COVID patients is quantified beyond the EHR visit-based case-ascertainment criteria themselves.
No Lyme disease content of any kind is present; this document cannot support any Lyme disease burden modeling, comparison, or crosscheck.

No caregiver time, household/family financial impact, or long-term (multi-year) financial consequence data are reported; the study's longest follow-up window used for incidence ascertainment is 270 days (harmonized analysis) or 180 days (main analysis), not a lifetime or multi-year cost horizon.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool the N3C (3,800,805 adults), PCORnet (1,870,810 adults), and PEDSnet (727,994 children) incidence estimates as a single range implying comparable measurement: each network applied a structurally different computable phenotype (N3C: machine-learning model trained on patients diagnosed with long COVID twice or with ≥2 long COVID clinic visits; PCORnet and PEDSnet: rules-based ICD-10 diagnosis-cluster algorithms) to different-sized, differently defined cohorts (adults vs. children).

Do not pool crude incidence proportion (10.2%-25.9% adults; 4.0% children) with excess incidence (5.3%-6.3% adults; 1.4% children) as if they were the same quantity at different confidence levels - excess incidence subtracts a COVID-negative control group's background rate and is explicitly presented by the authors as a 'lower bound' estimate, a conceptually different quantity from crude incidence.

The harmonized NASEM-aligned adult estimates (N3C 12.6%; PCORnet 9.6%) used a 270-day incidence window and were applied only to the two adult networks (not PEDSnet) - do not place these alongside the main 180-day-window estimates in a single low-to-high range without noting the different time window, different (harmonized) case definition, and exclusion of the pediatric network.

The 'historical' (Jan-May 2019) and 'contemporary' (Jan-May 2021) COVID-negative control groups are different populations drawn from different time periods used only to approximate a 'baseline' burden of long-COVID-like symptoms; the authors themselves note contemporary controls may have undocumented infections (understating the baseline) while historical controls may have different healthcare-utilization patterns (overstating the baseline) - neither should be treated as a nationally representative comparison population.

sex_gender_findings.finding: Across all three networks, female patients had a significantly higher adjusted risk of developing long COVID than male patients (N3C adjusted hazard ratio 1.41 [95% CI 1.41-1.42]; PCORnet adjusted hazard ratio 1.14 [1.12-1.14]; PEDSnet adjusted hazard ratio 1.17 [1.14-1.22]).

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: This study's long COVID case definitions are themselves built on ICD-10 diagnosis codes and EHR documentation: N3C's definition uses U09.9/B94.8 codes and a machine-learning model trained on patients diagnosed with U09.9 at least twice or who visited a long COVID clinic at least twice; PCORnet and PEDSnet use rules-based ICD-10 diagnosis-cluster algorithms. The document's own Limitations section states that EHR data 'may lead to underreporting or missed diagnoses of COVID-19 and long COVID, especially as patients must seek care as a prerequisite for having documentation available,' and that findings 'may also be influenced by...variation in healthcare access by gender, race/ethnicity, rurality, and other structural or social determinants of health.'

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document describes a classification/measurement-standard gap: there is no gold-standard, unified case definition for long COVID, each EHR research network built and applied its own computable phenotype, and the U09.9 ICD-10 code itself was introduced only partway through the study period with its adoption and use varying by healthcare institution - meaning no single, consistent diagnostic coding pathway existed across the health system during the study period.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: The document states: 'Given the lack of a gold standard, various case definitions for long COVID have been operationalized by researchers' (Introduction) and 'The code U09.9 was not appropriate for this purpose, as it was introduced during the study period and its adoption and use varies by healthcare institution' (Harmonized Long COVID Outcome Analysis, Methods).

federal_evidence_used.how_used: Used only to independently confirm that U09.9 (post COVID-19 condition) is the ICD-10-CM code referenced in this document's N3C/PCORnet/PEDSnet case definitions, and that B94.8 (sequelae of other specified infectious and parasitic diseases) is a nonspecific code also used in case ascertainment - supporting the claims_undercounting_caveat. This federal file contains no long COVID patient counts or costs and was not used to ground any crosscheck value.

spec.title: Long COVID Incidence After SARS-CoV-2 Infection: Comparing EHR Case-Definition Estimates (RECOVER N3C/PCORnet/PEDSnet)
spec.boundary: This simulator reproduces only the incidence-proportion estimates and adjusted hazard ratios reported in this EHR-based RECOVER cohort study (N3C, PCORnet, PEDSnet networks; COVID-19-positive patients with index events 2020-2023; outcomes assessed within 180 days of infection, except harmonized analyses which used 270 days and are not modeled here). It does not include any dollar cost, caregiving-time, insurance/access-barrier, or diagnostic-delay data, because the document reports none of these. It must not be used to infer Lyme disease burden, since Lyme disease is never discussed in the source. Crude incidence (not background-adjusted) and excess incidence (background-subtracted, labeled a 'lower bound' by the authors) are two structurally different quantities measured by two structurally different computable phenotypes (N3C: machine-learning model; PCORnet/PEDSnet: rules-based ICD-10 diagnosis-cluster algorithms); this simulator keeps them separate rather than pooling or averaging.

takeaway.patient: This study found that, depending on how researchers defined and measured long COVID in electronic health records, somewhere between about 10% and 26% of adults who had COVID-19 were later identified as having probable long COVID within 180 days, and about 4% of children were. After trying to subtract a background rate seen in people without COVID, the lower estimates were about 5-6% of adults and about 1.4% of children. The study also found women and people who were hospitalized, especially with ICU-level care, were at higher relative risk. These are different ways of counting the same underlying problem, not a single 'true' number - the right figure to focus on depends on what question you're asking.
takeaway.care: Across three large EHR research networks, crude long COVID identification ranged from 10.2% to 25.9% of COVID-19-positive adults and 4.0% of children, with a smaller 'excess' estimate (5.3-6.3% adults; 1.4% children) after background-rate adjustment. The near 2.5-fold spread between N3C's machine-learning phenotype and PCORnet's rules-based phenotype reflects case-definition design, not necessarily a true difference in patient populations. Adjusted hazard ratios of roughly 2.0-2.8x for ICU-level hospitalization versus no hospitalization (varying by network) suggest a workflow opportunity for targeted post-COVID follow-up, though the authors note closer inpatient follow-up could itself inflate detection.
takeaway.policy: This study provides three non-interchangeable incidence bounds for adult long COVID: crude EHR-identified incidence (10.2-25.9%), background-adjusted excess incidence (5.3-6.3%, the authors' own conservative lower bound), and a harmonized 270-day NASEM-aligned estimate (9.6-12.6%, not modeled in this simulator). Pediatric crude incidence was 4.0% (excess 1.4%). No decline in incidence was observed through January 2024. Because EHR/ICD-10-based case definitions require documented care-seeking, and the U09.9 code was introduced only partway through the study period with institution-dependent adoption, these figures likely undercount true long COVID burden and should not be treated as a ceiling.

patient: If you were hospitalized, especially with ICU-level care, during a COVID-19 infection, consider asking your clinician whether a structured check-in for lingering symptoms makes sense, since the study found hospitalized/ICU patients had a notably higher relative risk of long COVID.

Know that different studies may report different percentages (for example 10% vs 26% of adults) depending on how 'long COVID' was defined in that study - this doesn't mean one number is simply wrong, so it's worth asking which definition is being used when you see a statistic.
If you are a woman, note the study found a somewhat higher relative risk than for men across all three groups studied, though this describes a group-level pattern, not an individual prediction.

Because the study looked at symptoms appearing within about 6 months of infection, tracking how you feel over that window after any future COVID infection may be useful context to bring to a clinician.
care: Consider using the hazard-ratio gradient (roughly 2.0-2.8x higher risk after ICU-level hospitalization versus no hospitalization, varying by network) to inform prioritization of structured post-COVID follow-up outreach, while keeping in mind the authors' own caveat that closer inpatient follow-up may itself inflate detection rates.

This finding may be worth checking against your own workflow: review how your EHR/coding system identifies long COVID cases (e.g., reliance on ICD-10 code U09.9 introduced mid-pandemic with variable adoption) and whether that could be under- or over-capturing cases compared to a clinical judgment-based approach.

Given the reported sex difference in adjusted risk (women higher than men in all three networks, though the size of that difference varied by network), it may be worth discussing whether post-COVID symptom screening in your pathway is applied consistently regardless of patient sex.

Since the two adult networks' crude estimates differed by roughly 2.5-fold using different algorithms, treat any single incidence number from this study as model-dependent rather than a fixed capacity-planning figure.
policy: Use the crude (10.2%-25.9%) and excess (5.3%-6.3%) adult incidence estimates as explicit low/high bounds in capacity or burden-modeling exercises rather than averaging them into one point estimate.

Consider supporting work toward a standardized, harmonized long COVID case definition, given that the study's own 2.5-fold difference between networks appears attributable to differing computable-phenotype design rather than to a real difference in the underlying COVID-19 populations studied.

Factor the reported hospitalization/ICU-level hazard ratios (approximately 2.0x-2.8x across the three networks) into risk-based targeting for post-COVID program funding, while noting the authors' caveat that greater clinical follow-up of inpatients may partly inflate these estimates.

Treat EHR/claims-based incidence figures as a likely undercount of true long COVID burden, since case ascertainment depends on patients seeking and receiving documented care, and weigh this when deciding how much additional population-level surveillance investment is warranted.

## Source and scope
This simulator is built from a peer-reviewed RECOVER Initiative EHR cohort study using three U.S. research networks: N3C (3,800,805 adults), PCORnet (1,870,810 adults), and PEDSnet (727,994 children, age ≤21), covering COVID-19-positive patients with index events from March 2020 through July 2023, with long COVID outcomes assessed within 180 days of infection (Results, p.1252; Table 2). The study reports no dollar costs, caregiving time, or access-barrier data of any kind.

## Two measurement constructs, not one
N3C used a machine-learning model trained on patients diagnosed with U09.9 at least twice or with ≥2 long COVID clinic visits; PCORnet and PEDSnet used rules-based ICD-10 diagnosis-cluster algorithms. These produced crude incidence of 10.2% (N3C), 25.9% (PCORnet) in adults and 4.0% (PEDSnet) in children. 'Excess incidence' (5.3%, 6.3%, and 1.4% respectively) further subtracts a COVID-negative control group's background rate and is explicitly labeled a conservative lower bound by the authors (Control Group Analysis, p.1257). Crude and excess incidence measure different things and should not be averaged or treated as the same quantity at different confidence levels.

## Risk subgroups
Adjusted hazard ratios for long COVID following ICU-level hospitalization versus no hospitalization were 2.04 (N3C), 2.19 (PCORnet), and 2.83 (PEDSnet), all p<.001 (Multivariable Analysis, p.1255; Table 3). Female patients had significantly higher adjusted risk than male patients in all three networks (N3C aHR 1.41 [1.41-1.42]; PCORnet aHR 1.14 [1.12-1.14]; PEDSnet aHR 1.17 [1.14-1.22]), a sex-based difference consistent across networks though of differing magnitude.

## Limitations
This study's case definitions rely on ICD-10 codes (U09.9, B94.8) and EHR documentation; the authors state EHR data 'may lead to underreporting or missed diagnoses...especially as patients must seek care as a prerequisite for having documentation available,' so these figures likely undercount true long COVID prevalence, particularly where healthcare access varies by gender, race/ethnicity, or rurality.

Separately, the study identifies a measurement-system gap: there is no gold-standard long COVID case definition, each network built its own computable phenotype, and the U09.9 code itself was introduced only partway through the study period with institution-dependent adoption - meaning no single consistent diagnostic coding pathway existed system-wide during this period.

Harmonized NASEM-aligned 270-day estimates (N3C 12.6%, PCORnet 9.6%) and historical/contemporary control-group details are reported in the source but not modeled in this simulator.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

- Crude long COVID incidence proportion among COVID-19-positive adults, N3C computable phenotype (2020-2023): the document reports 10.2% as the share of adults who ever had COVID-19 that ever experienced Long COVID; the national survey's 18 wave(s) in that period ranged from 25.6% to 35.1% (interval bounds 24.9% to 36%), so the document's figure is below every survey wave interval in that period. The survey is self-reported adults; a different definition or population in the document makes a gap expected, so treat it as a prompt to check. Federal source: household survey (self-report), 2022-2024; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Crude long COVID incidence proportion among COVID-19-positive adults, PCORnet computable phenotype (2020-2023): the document reports 25.9% as the share of adults who ever had COVID-19 that ever experienced Long COVID; the national survey's 18 wave(s) in that period ranged from 25.6% to 35.1% (interval bounds 24.9% to 36%), so the document's figure is inside the published 95% interval of at least one survey wave. The survey is self-reported adults; a different definition or population in the document makes a gap expected, so treat it as a prompt to check. Federal source: household survey (self-report), 2022-2024; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Harmonized NASEM-aligned long COVID incidence proportion among COVID-19-positive adults, N3C (2020-2023): the document reports 12.6% as the share of adults who ever had COVID-19 that ever experienced Long COVID; the national survey's 18 wave(s) in that period ranged from 25.6% to 35.1% (interval bounds 24.9% to 36%), so the document's figure is below every survey wave interval in that period. spec.title: Long COVID Incidence After SARS-CoV-2 Infection: Comparing EHR Case-Definition Estimates (RECOVER N3C/PCORnet/PEDSnet)
spec.boundary: This simulator reproduces only the incidence-proportion estimates and adjusted hazard ratios reported in this EHR-based RECOVER cohort study (N3C, PCORnet, PEDSnet networks; COVID-19-positive patients with index events 2020-2023; outcomes assessed within 180 days of infection, except harmonized analyses which used 270 days and are not modeled here). It does not include any dollar cost, caregiving-time, insurance/access-barrier, or diagnostic-delay data, because the document reports none of these. It must not be used to infer Lyme disease burden, since Lyme disease is never discussed in the source. Crude incidence (not background-adjusted) and excess incidence (background-subtracted, labeled a 'lower bound' by the authors) are two structurally different quantities measured by two structurally different computable phenotypes (N3C: machine-learning model; PCORnet/PEDSnet: rules-based ICD-10 diagnosis-cluster algorithms); this simulator keeps them separate rather than pooling or averaging.

takeaway.patient: This study found that, depending on how researchers defined and measured long COVID in electronic health records, somewhere between about 10% and 26% of adults who had COVID-19 were later identified as having probable long COVID within 180 days, and about 4% of children were. After trying to subtract a background rate seen in people without COVID, the lower estimates were about 5-6% of adults and about 1.4% of children. The study also found women and people who were hospitalized, especially with ICU-level care, were at higher relative risk. These are different ways of counting the same underlying problem, not a single 'true' number - the right figure to focus on depends on what question you're asking.
takeaway.care: Across three large EHR research networks, crude long COVID identification ranged from 10.2% to 25.9% of COVID-19-positive adults and 4.0% of children, with a smaller 'excess' estimate (5.3-6.3% adults; 1.4% children) after background-rate adjustment. The near 2.5-fold spread between N3C's machine-learning phenotype and PCORnet's rules-based phenotype reflects case-definition design, not necessarily a true difference in patient populations. Adjusted hazard ratios of roughly 2.0-2.8x for ICU-level hospitalization versus no hospitalization (varying by network) suggest a workflow opportunity for targeted post-COVID follow-up, though the authors note closer inpatient follow-up could itself inflate detection.
takeaway.policy: This study provides three non-interchangeable incidence bounds for adult long COVID: crude EHR-identified incidence (10.2-25.9%), background-adjusted excess incidence (5.3-6.3%, the authors' own conservative lower bound), and a harmonized 270-day NASEM-aligned estimate (9.6-12.6%, not modeled in this simulator). Pediatric crude incidence was 4.0% (excess 1.4%). No decline in incidence was observed through January 2024. Because EHR/ICD-10-based case definitions require documented care-seeking, and the U09.9 code was introduced only partway through the study period with institution-dependent adoption, these figures likely undercount true long COVID burden and should not be treated as a ceiling.

patient: If you were hospitalized, especially with ICU-level care, during a COVID-19 infection, consider asking your clinician whether a structured check-in for lingering symptoms makes sense, since the study found hospitalized/ICU patients had a notably higher relative risk of long COVID.

Know that different studies may report different percentages (for example 10% vs 26% of adults) depending on how 'long COVID' was defined in that study - this doesn't mean one number is simply wrong, so it's worth asking which definition is being used when you see a statistic.
If you are a woman, note the study found a somewhat higher relative risk than for men across all three groups studied, though this describes a group-level pattern, not an individual prediction.

Because the study looked at symptoms appearing within about 6 months of infection, tracking how you feel over that window after any future COVID infection may be useful context to bring to a clinician.
care: Consider using the hazard-ratio gradient (roughly 2.0-2.8x higher risk after ICU-level hospitalization versus no hospitalization, varying by network) to inform prioritization of structured post-COVID follow-up outreach, while keeping in mind the authors' own caveat that closer inpatient follow-up may itself inflate detection rates.

This finding may be worth checking against your own workflow: review how your EHR/coding system identifies long COVID cases (e.g., reliance on ICD-10 code U09.9 introduced mid-pandemic with variable adoption) and whether that could be under- or over-capturing cases compared to a clinical judgment-based approach.

Given the reported sex difference in adjusted risk (women higher than men in all three networks, though the size of that difference varied by network), it may be worth discussing whether post-COVID symptom screening in your pathway is applied consistently regardless of patient sex.

Since the two adult networks' crude estimates differed by roughly 2.5-fold using different algorithms, treat any single incidence number from this study as model-dependent rather than a fixed capacity-planning figure.
policy: Use the crude (10.2%-25.9%) and excess (5.3%-6.3%) adult incidence estimates as explicit low/high bounds in capacity or burden-modeling exercises rather than averaging them into one point estimate.

Consider supporting work toward a standardized, harmonized long COVID case definition, given that the study's own 2.5-fold difference between networks appears attributable to differing computable-phenotype design rather than to a real difference in the underlying COVID-19 populations studied.

Factor the reported hospitalization/ICU-level hazard ratios (approximately 2.0x-2.8x across the three networks) into risk-based targeting for post-COVID program funding, while noting the authors' caveat that greater clinical follow-up of inpatients may partly inflate these estimates.

Treat EHR/claims-based incidence figures as a likely undercount of true long COVID burden, since case ascertainment depends on patients seeking and receiving documented care, and weigh this when deciding how much additional population-level surveillance investment is warranted.

inputs.source: Results, p.1252; Table 2. 1-10 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.

inputs.interpretation: This is N3C's adjusted hazard ratio for developing long COVID after ICU-level hospitalization versus no hospitalization; a higher value means hospitalization/ICU care was associated with a stronger relative risk in this network's data, though the authors note closer inpatient follow-up could itself inflate detection.

outputs.label: N3C crude minus excess adult incidence (positive = crude estimate exceeds the excess/background-adjusted estimate; negative = excess exceeds crude, not expected under the study's method but shown for exploration)
outputs.interpretation: This is the gap between N3C's crude long COVID incidence and its own lower-bound excess-incidence estimate after subtracting a COVID-negative control group's background rate; a larger gap means more of the crude estimate may reflect background symptom reporting rather than COVID-specific illness, per the document's own framing of excess incidence as a conservative lower bound.

outputs.label: PCORnet crude minus excess adult incidence (positive = crude estimate exceeds the excess/background-adjusted estimate; negative = excess exceeds crude, not expected under the study's method but shown for exploration)
outputs.interpretation: This is the same type of gap calculated from PCORnet's own crude and excess estimates; comparing it with N3C's equivalent gap shows whether the two networks' background-adjustment procedures lead to similar or different conclusions about how much of the crude estimate is COVID-specific.

outputs.label: PEDSnet crude minus excess pediatric incidence (positive = crude estimate exceeds the excess/background-adjusted estimate; negative = excess exceeds crude, not expected under the study's method but shown for exploration)
outputs.interpretation: This is the equivalent gap for children; the document reports a smaller crude pediatric estimate (4.0%) than either adult network's crude estimate, so this gap shows how much of that smaller figure the authors attribute to background rates versus COVID-specific illness.

outputs.label: PCORnet crude adult incidence minus N3C crude adult incidence (positive = PCORnet's rules-based definition identifies a higher share of patients as long COVID than N3C's ML-based definition; negative would mean the reverse)
outputs.interpretation: This quantifies the documented spread between the two adult networks' crude incidence estimates (25.9% vs 10.2%), which the authors attribute to differences in computable-phenotype design (machine-learning vs rules-based) rather than to the two cohorts being genuinely different populations; a larger value means case-definition choice is driving more of the apparent difference in who counts as having long COVID.

outputs.label: Adjusted hazard ratio for long COVID after ICU-level hospitalization vs. no hospitalization (N3C), shown directly
outputs.interpretation: This repeats the N3C adjusted hazard ratio input as a direct output; a value above 1 means ICU-level hospitalization was associated with a higher rate of developing long COVID relative to not being hospitalized. Comparable adjusted hazard ratios were reported for PCORnet (2.19) and PEDSnet (2.83) but are not modeled in this output.
